t: Can Make Palindrome from Substring — Prefix Bitmask Counting
o: For each query we may **rearrange** the substring, so only character counts matter — a substring can be made a palindrome iff at most one character has an odd count (for even length: zero odd counts; for odd length: exactly one). Each replacement of a letter can fix two odd-count characters at once (turn one occurrence of an over-represented letter into a missing one), so the answer is `true` iff `oddCount / 2 <= k`. In example 1, `"abcd"` has 4 odd counts, needing 2 replacements: `k=1` fails, `k=2` succeeds; `"abcda"` has 3 odds, needing 1 replacement, so `k=1` succeeds. With up to $10^5$ queries and strings of length $10^5$, recounting each substring naively is $O(q \cdot n)$ — too slow in the worst case, so we need per-query $O(1)$ or $O(26)$ work after linear preprocessing.
k: Rearrangement means only parity of character counts matters: a multiset forms a palindrome iff the number of letters with odd count is 0 or 1.
Each replacement fixes two odd-count letters simultaneously, so the minimum replacements needed is floor(oddCount / 2).
Store prefix parities as a 26-bit mask; the parity of any substring is `prefix[right+1] ^ prefix[left]`, giving O(1) queries.
popcount of that mask gives the number of odd-count characters directly.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Counting Per Query
a.i: For each query, directly count occurrences of each of the 26 letters in the substring, then compute how many have odd counts. The needed replacements are half that number. This is simple and correct but costs O(length) per query, which can be too slow for large inputs.
s: For each query [l, r, k], iterate i from l to r incrementing cnt[s[i]-'a'].
Count how many of the 26 buckets are odd.
a.t: O(q · n) time — each query scans its whole substring; worst case ~10^10 operations, too slow for maximum constraints but fine for small inputs.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the output — a fixed 26-element counter per query.

a.i: Precompute prefix[i] = bitmask where bit c is set iff letter c appears an odd number of times in s[0..i-1]. Then the parity mask of any substring s[l..r] is prefix[r+1] ^ prefix[l], since common prefix bits cancel. The popcount of this mask equals the number of odd-count letters, so each query is answered in O(1): check popcount/2 <= k.
s: Build array pre of length n+1 with pre[0]=0; pre[i+1] = pre[i] ^ (1 << (s[i]-'a')).
For each query [l, r, k], compute mask = pre[r+1] ^ pre[l].
Let odd = popcount(mask); answer true iff odd/2 <= k.
a.t: O(n + q) time — O(n) to build prefix masks, O(1) per query via bit operations.
a.sp: O(n) space for the prefix mask array plus the output list.

w: In an interview, state the rearrangement insight first (only parities matter), derive the odd/2 <= k condition, then optimize from per-query counting to prefix XOR masks. Common pitfalls: forgetting that a replacement changes one letter's parity twice (fixing two odds at once), mishandling single-character substrings (always palindromes, odd=1 needs 0 replacements — the formula handles it), and using a full 26-int count table per query instead of a bitmask. Edge cases: k=0, left==right, all-identical substrings. Follow-ups: what if replacements were limited to specific letters, or if the string could be updated between queries (then consider a BIT over masks or sqrt decomposition).
